article_content: A former West Yorkshire Police inspector faces formal investigation for allegedly acting on behalf of deceased paedophile Jimmy Savile by contacting Surrey Police prior to his 2009 interview regarding historical sex abuse allegations. Released transcripts revealed detectives adopted a lenient approach during the 56-minute interview, despite evidence of Savile's predatory behavior toward teenage girls at Staines' Duncroft School. Ex-officer Paul Leonard described witnessing Savile with underage individuals and being warned by superiors about the DJ's influential connections. Savile referenced his 'Friday Morning Club' meetings with senior officers during the interview, dismissing allegations as blackmail attempts. Survivors such as Jill Bartlett (raped at 16) and Sylvia Edwards (attacked on Top of the Pops) demanded independent investigations into police conduct. West Yorkshire's Operation Newgreen report found no systemic protection, though critics like ex-detective Mark Williams-Thomas called it inadequate. The IPCC confirmed launching an investigation into the inspector's pre-interview communications with Surrey Police.

article_content: While watching 'Lincoln,' Connecticut Representative Joe Courtney was surprised to see the film show his state's 1865 representatives opposing the 13th Amendment - contrary to historical records proving their unanimous support. He formally protested this inaccuracy to director Steven Spielberg and screenwriter Tony Kushner, who acknowledged taking creative liberties to build suspense around the amendment's uncertain fate. Kushner defended dramatizations as standard in historical filmmaking, noting invented characters and dialogues were used to enhance storytelling. Historians agree the film broadly captures the amendment's legislative struggle, though they criticize the Connecticut error as unnecessary. The controversy underscores challenges in balancing historical precision with cinematic narrative needs.

article_content: President Barack Obama's nomination of Judge Sonia Sotomayor reflects a deliberate prioritization of legal expertise over political experience. Her academic excellence (Princeton summa cum laude, Yale Law editor) combined with 17 years on the Second Circuit Court positions her uniquely to handle the Supreme Court's technical caseload. While historical figures like Chief Justice Taft demonstrated political leaders can succeed, the contemporary Court's workflow requires intimate knowledge of procedural minutiae. Take a recent case involving taxpayer liability under the Federal Arbitration Act: resolving whether non-signatories could appeal arbitration stays demands precise statutory interpretation unfamiliar to most politicians. Though empathy informs judicial philosophy, the author stresses that technical mastery forms the bedrock of constitutional adjudication. Sotomayor's career progression - from prosecutor to trial judge to appellate jurist - provides the framework necessary to balance legal principles with societal implications, making her a fitting 'inside-the-box' choice despite calls for unconventional selections.

article_content: Cambridge United hero Ryan Donaldson couldn't hide his delight after securing a 'dream' Old Trafford replay following his side's 0-0 draw against Manchester United in the FA Cup on Friday night. The winger was named man-of-the-match as the League Two side held the Red Devils in their fourth-round tie, praising his team-mates for the hard-fought result. 'It was hard! Really hard. We got pinned back, but they have world-class players and a draw is a dream result for us,' he said. Cambridge United team-mates Ryan Donaldson (left) and Tom Champion celebrated at full-time. Donaldson, the match-winner, expressed delight at earning a 'dream' replay at Old Trafford. 'They had two great chances in the second half and we’ll take a draw any day. It’s going to be surreal at Old Trafford, but we’ve been to Wembley twice last year—not bad, is it?' 'I thought it was quite an even game in terms of chances. We’ll take this. It’s incredible. We’ve played at Wembley before and the gaffer has been saying all season that this cup run can give us those moments again. 'How many people will we take to Old Trafford? 15,000? I don’t know. Whatever tickets we get, we’ll sell out, I’m sure.' Meanwhile, Cambridge United boss Richard Money praised his side’s performance. 'I’m extremely proud of every single one of my players,' he said. 'In the first half we carried a threat. In the second half it became world-class players keeping the ball, but our organization was good and we defended well. We needed the goalkeeper and center-backs to be solid, and they were. 'We tried to make sure the game didn’t faze them in the tunnel. Look at the badge and go out to work hard and see what happens. We were confident we could compete. We’ll take the replay of course.'

article_content: Archaeologists have uncovered a Viking warrior whose filed teeth reveal a brutal rite of passage. Discovered in a mass grave in Weymouth, Dorset, the remains show deliberate grooves in the front teeth—likely performed without anesthesia—to intimidate enemies or signify combat prowess. The burial pit, dated between 970–1025 CE, contains 51 skulls and 54 bodies, many decapitated with multiple blade injuries. Isotope analysis of a severed jaw's teeth confirms Nordic origins, suggesting these warriors were executed by Anglo-Saxons after a battle. While such dental modification is rare in European archaeological records, similar practices exist globally, offering new insights into Viking warrior culture and identity.

article_content: A plasterer fatally stabbed his identical twin brother during a New Year's Eve argument using a kitchen knife before attending a party, Winchester Crown Court heard. Robert Cerqua, 31, allegedly attacked his carpenter brother Christopher at their parents' Hythe home after disputes over past conflicts. Emergency services received a 13-minute 999 call from the parents pleading for help as Christopher lay bleeding from a seven-inch abdominal wound that pierced his aorta. Despite the father's efforts to stem bleeding with a tea towel, Christopher suffered a cardiac arrest and died in hospital. Robert left barefoot, attended a party until 2:20 AM, and disabled his phone. Police located him at a Totton gathering, where he reacted with confusion upon arrest, repeatedly questioning whether he'd killed his brother. Forensic analysis confirmed the fatal injury caused massive internal bleeding. Robert claims self-defense after his brother allegedly threatened him with the knife, but prosecutors argue the act resulted from intentional aggression. The trial continues.
